About us

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand - Te Pūtea Matua is New Zealand’s central bank. Toitū Te, Toitū Te Ōranga - we enable economic wellbeing and prosperity for all New Zealanders. We have a clear goal – to create an environment that fosters the overall economic wellbeing of the country and the living standards of all New Zealanders so that we, and generations to come, continue to enjoy this great country. Our mandates are: - maintaining low and stable consumer price inflation while contributing to maximum sustainable employment; - promoting and maintaining a sound and efficient financial system; - meeting the cash needs of the public; - and providing robust payment and settlement services for New Zealand’s financial institutions.

    Reserve Bank Governor Anna Breman has appointed Angus McGregor as Assistant Governor Financial Stability, following an extensive recruitment process. Mr McGregor joined the Reserve Bank of New Zealand in 2022 and has been Acting Assistant Governor Financial Stability since March 2025. Governor Breman says he brings deep experience and proven leadership to one of the Bank’s most senior and visible roles. Angus has built trusted relationships across the financial sector, both in New Zealand and internationally, and is highly regarded by stakeholders and peers. He has also led significant enforcement work, including successful outcomes in recent court action.

    Celebrating 1-year of the Depositor Compensation Scheme (DCS) protecting your money. The DCS protects your money in the unlikely event that your deposit taker fails. Coverage is up to $100,000 per person, per deposit taker, and is automatic if your money is in DCS-protected accounts. The DCS covers money held at deposit takers like ⬇️ • Banks • Building societies • Credit unions • Finance companies that take retail deposits Visit dcs.govt.nz to learn more

    Earlier this month, our senior leaders have been out across the regions with Assistant Governor Karen Silk visiting Tauranga and Chief Economist Paul Conway visiting Rotorua.   In Tauranga, Karen met with a range of local businesses and regional leaders across key export, infrastructure, and development sectors. In Rotorua, Paul engaged with the bio-economy, forestry operators, and local business groups to better understand conditions across the region.   These regional engagements are an important part of how we operate at the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. They provide an opportunity to step beyond the data, hear directly how economic conditions are being experienced on the ground, and strengthen our understanding of the diverse drivers shaping regional economies.   While each region and sector has its own distinct context, a consistent set of themes emerged across visits, particularly around adaptation and resilience.   We would like to thank everyone who took the time to meet with us and share their insights. These discussions help to inform our thinking and ensuring we remain closely connected to the economy we serve.

    We have opened consultations on a package of crisis preparedness policies for deposit takers alongside the final tranche of the Deposit Takers Act 2023 (DTA) draft standards and guidance. We are seeking feedback from interested stakeholders. The crisis preparedness policies are designed to enable the orderly resolution of a deposit taker failure, while preserving critical customer services and avoiding the use of public funds. The DTA standards consultation package includes exposure drafts and guidance of the: • Capital Standard • Internal Models Standard (requirements relevant only to deposit takers that use the Internal Ratings-Based model) • Operational Resilience Standard • Outsourcing Standard • Disclosure Standard (remaining aspects not covered in tranche 2 consultation) • Related Party Exposures Standard. This is the third and final tranche of DTA draft standards and guidance that will be issued in 2027. Crisis preparedness standards will be issued separately in 2028. Submissions close at 5pm on Friday 11 September 2026. Find the consultations here: https://lnkd.in/e68fkuEQ

    All New Zealand deposit takers licensed under the Deposit Takers Act 2023 will be able to call themselves banks. Use of the words ‘bank’, ‘banker’ and ‘banking’ are restricted to help the public identify prudentially regulated entities.   From 1 December 2028, all licensed deposit takers, including current non-bank deposit takers, will be able to use these restricted words. Overseas banks without a physical presence in New Zealand can continue to use restricted words, as is authorised under the Act.   The change supports a more consistent framework across the sector and was largely supported in consultation. Read more here: https://lnkd.in/eZ2a2ik5

    Most of us hope for the best but plan for the worst – and that’s what stress testing does. If you have savings in the bank, or insurance for your house, car or contents, you might be wondering if banks and insurers are prepared for the “what if?” events - like a sharp fall in house prices, a major natural disaster, or a global conflict. We keep a close eye on banks and insurers to see how they would cope in severe economic situations. Our stress tests check whether they are strong enough to get through tough or unexpected scenarios. Stress testing ensures your everyday financial services remain reliable – so you know your insurance claims can be paid, banks can keep lending even in hard times, your deposits stay safe, and the wider financial system is stable. Learn more here: https://lnkd.in/egExzi7G
